title: Behavioural Diversity and Ecology of Cleaning Mutualisms in a Changing Ocean
content:
Cleaning mutualisms sustain coral reef health, but anthropogenic stressors—from ocean acidification to fishing pressure—are reshaping them. These pressures drive molecular, physiological, cognitive, and behavioural changes in cleaners and clients, reducing cleaning frequency and quality. The resulting cascade—rising parasite loads, declining client health, and reduced recruitment—threatens reef biodiversity, raising urgent questions about the resilience of cleaning mutualisms under intensifying global change.


ABSTRACT

One of the most pressing challenges confronting the scientific community today is understanding the consequences of global change on ecological communities and mitigating their impacts. Cleaning mutualisms are essential to the health and stability of coral reef ecosystems, influencing individual fitness, parasite dynamics, and community composition. However, these interactions are increasingly threatened by anthropogenic pressures. This review describes the behavioural diversity and ecology of dedicated cleaners, ranging from cognitively sophisticated wrasses and efficient, low-conflict gobies to visually signalling shrimps. We then review how the intricate interactions between cleaners and clients respond to environmental change, including chronic stressors (e.g., acidification), extreme events (e.g., marine heatwaves), and direct anthropogenic disturbances (e.g., underwater noise). Mounting evidence demonstrates that such stressors can disrupt cleaner and client dynamics, diminishing interaction motivation and quality, and altering underlying neurobiological mechanisms. Despite recent advances, significant gaps remain in our understanding of the long-term resilience and recovery of cleaning mutualisms across ecological, behavioural, cognitive and physiological pathways. As ocean climate-related drivers of change intensify and increasingly co-occur, it becomes urgent to investigate whether cleaners can continue to fulfil their ecological roles, or if reefs will face a future with compromised mutualistic services.
